lessons.title: Cost of Production and Profitability Analysis
lessons.body: To know if your sweet potato farming is making money, you must track every cost. Start by listing all expenses for one acre (0.4 hectares). Common costs in Africa include: land preparation (ploughing and harrowing) â $50-100; vines (cuttings) â $30-60 for 10,000-15,000 cuttings; planting labour â $40-80; weeding (2-3 times) â $60-120; fertiliser (if used) â $50-150; pest control â $20-50; harvesting labour â $50-100; and transport to market â $20-60. Total costs can range from $300 to $700 per acre. Your yield also matters: with good practices, you can harvest 5-10 tonnes per acre. If you sell at $0.20 per kg (a typical farmgate price), 7 tonnes gives $1,400 revenue. Subtract $500 costs, and your profit is $900. But if you sell at $0.10 per kg, revenue is only $700, and profit drops to $200. To improve profitability, focus on reducing costs (e.g., use own vines, compost instead of bought fertiliser) and increasing yield (use improved varieties like Naspot 1 or Vita). Also consider value addition: selling processed chips or flour can double your price. Always calculate your break-even point: total costs divided by price per kg gives the minimum kg you must sell. For example, $500 costs Ã· $0.20 = 2,500 kg. If you harvest more than that, you make a profit. Keep records of all costs and sales to know your true profit.

lessons.title: Record Keeping and Financial Planning
lessons.body: Record keeping is the backbone of a profitable sweet potato farm. Without records, you are farming blind. You need three simple books: a cash book, a labour record, and a harvest log. In your cash book, write down every amount you spend or receive, with date and reason. For example: '5 May â bought 10,000 vines â $50'. For labour, note who worked, how many hours, and what you paid. For harvest, record the date, plot, variety, and weight harvested. Use a simple notebook or a free app like 'Farm Records' on your phone. At the end of each season, calculate your total income and total expenses. This shows your profit or loss. Financial planning means looking ahead. Before planting, estimate your costs and expected income. If you plan to plant one acre, you know you need about $500. You can save little by little each week, or take a small loan from a SACCO or village savings group. Also plan for reinvestment: set aside 20% of profit for next season's inputs. For example, if you make $900 profit, save $180 for vines and fertiliser. Keep a separate bank account or mobile money wallet for farm money to avoid mixing with household cash. Finally, review your records each year to see where you can cut costs or increase yields. Good records help you get loans, because lenders want to see your numbers. They also help you negotiate better prices when you know your true cost of production.

lessons.title: Sustainable Practices: Crop Rotation and Cover Crops
lessons.body: Sweet potatoes take a lot of nutrients from the soil, especially potassium. If you plant them in the same plot year after year, yields drop and pests build up. Crop rotation means changing what you grow in each plot each season. A good rotation for sweet potatoes is: Year 1 â sweet potatoes; Year 2 â maize or sorghum; Year 3 â legumes like beans or groundnuts; then back to sweet potatoes. Legumes fix nitrogen in the soil, which helps the next crop. This rotation reduces soil-borne diseases like sweet potato weevils and nematodes. Cover crops are plants grown to protect and improve the soil, not for harvest. Examples are mucuna (velvet bean), lablab, and cowpeas. Plant them after harvesting sweet potatoes. They cover the ground, prevent erosion, and add organic matter when you plough them back in. You can also use sweet potato vines themselves as a cover crop â they spread quickly and suppress weeds. Another sustainable practice is mulching with dry grass or crop residues. This keeps moisture in the soil, reduces weeding, and adds nutrients as it decomposes. Compost is also key: make a pile of kitchen waste, crop residues, and animal manure. Turn it every two weeks. After two months, it becomes dark, rich compost. Apply 2-3 tonnes per acre before planting. These practices cost little but maintain soil health for years. They also reduce your need for expensive chemical fertilisers, saving you money and protecting the environment.

lessons.title: Organic Certification and Good Agricultural Practices (GAP)
lessons.body: Organic certification means your sweet potatoes are grown without synthetic chemicals and meet specific standards. It can open export markets and fetch higher prices, but it requires strict record-keeping and a 2-3 year transition period. To start, contact a local certification body like Ecocert or Ceres. They will inspect your farm and check your practices. You must avoid all synthetic pesticides and fertilisers. Instead, use compost, manure, and natural pest control like neem extract or wood ash. You also need buffer zones to prevent chemical drift from neighbouring farms. The cost of certification can be $500-$2000 per year, so it is best done through a cooperative to share costs. Good Agricultural Practices (GAP) are a set of standards for safe and sustainable farming. They are often required by supermarkets and processors. Key GAP rules include: use clean water for irrigation; keep animals out of the field; wash hands and tools; store chemicals safely (if allowed); and keep records of all inputs and harvests. For sweet potatoes, GAP also means careful handling to avoid bruising, and curing roots after harvest (keeping them in a warm, humid place for 4-7 days) to heal cuts and extend shelf life. Many African countries have national GAP guidelines â check with your extension officer. Even if you do not get certified, following GAP improves quality and reduces waste. It also makes your produce more attractive to buyers who care about food safety.

lessons.title: Accessing Markets and Cooperatives
lessons.body: Finding a reliable market is as important as growing a good crop. Start by identifying who buys sweet potatoes in your area: local traders, supermarkets, schools, hospitals, or processors making chips or flour. Visit them and ask about their requirements: volume, quality, timing, and price. For example, a supermarket may want 500 kg per week, washed and graded, and pay $0.30 per kg. A local trader might buy ungraded at $0.15 per kg but collect from your farm. To get better prices, join or form a cooperative. A cooperative pools members' produce to meet large orders. For instance, 20 farmers each with 1 tonne can supply 20 tonnes to a processor. That gives you bargaining power. Cooperatives also help with transport, storage, and access to loans. To form one, register with the ministry of cooperatives â it usually costs a small fee. You need a constitution, elected leaders, and a bank account. Another option is contract farming: sign an agreement with a buyer before planting. They may provide vines or inputs, and you agree to sell to them at a set price. This reduces risk. Also consider value addition: making sweet potato chips, flour, or animal feed can increase your income. For example, fresh roots sell for $0.20 per kg, but dried chips can sell for $0.50 per kg. Start small, test the market, and scale up as you learn.

lessons.title: Developing a Sweet Potato Farming Business Plan
lessons.body: A business plan is a roadmap for your sweet potato farm. It helps you get loans, plan your season, and measure success. Start with a one-page summary: your name, location, what you will produce, and how much money you need. Then describe your farm: size (e.g., 2 acres), soil type, water source, and equipment. Next, outline your production plan: which varieties (e.g., Naspot 1 for high yield, Kabode for orange flesh), planting dates, spacing (30 cm between plants, 1 m between ridges), and expected yield (8 tonnes per acre). Include a budget: costs for land prep, vines, labour, fertiliser, and transport. For 2 acres, total costs might be $1,200. Then project income: 16 tonnes at $0.25 per kg = $4,000. Profit = $2,800. Show your marketing plan: who will buy, at what price, and how you will deliver. For example, sell 10 tonnes to a local trader at $0.20 and 6 tonnes to a school at $0.30. Include a risk plan: what if drought hits? You will use mulching and a small irrigation pump. What if prices fall? You will store and sell later, or process into chips. Finally, include a timeline: month-by-month activities from land preparation to harvest and sales. Review your plan every season and adjust based on records. A good plan is simple, realistic, and written down. Share it with your family and cooperative for feedback. With a solid plan, you can turn sweet potato farming into a profitable business.

quiz.q: What is the first step in calculating profitability for sweet potato farming?
quiz.explanation: You must know your total costs before you can determine profit.

quiz.q: If your total cost per acre is $500 and you sell 7 tonnes at $0.20 per kg, what is your profit?
Which of these is a variable cost in sweet potato production?
quiz.explanation: Planting labour changes with the size of the farm and season, so it is variable.

quiz.q: What is the break-even point in kg if total costs are $600 and price is $0.30 per kg?
Why is value addition important for profitability?
options: B) It increases the selling price
C) It requires no extra work
quiz.explanation: Processing into chips or flour can double the price per kg.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a cash book?
options: A) To record every income and expense
quiz.explanation: A cash book tracks all money coming in and going out.

quiz.q: Which record helps you know how much you paid for labour?
quiz.explanation: Labour record details work done, and cash book shows payments.

quiz.q: What percentage of profit is recommended to set aside for next season's inputs?
quiz.explanation: Saving 20% helps you reinvest without borrowing.

quiz.q: Why should you keep farm money separate from household cash?
options: A) To avoid mixing and losing track
B) To hide it from family
quiz.explanation: Separate accounts prevent accidental spending of farm funds.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of good record keeping?
options: A) It helps you get loans
quiz.explanation: Lenders want to see your financial records before giving loans.

quiz.q: Which crop is a good legume for rotation with sweet potatoes?
quiz.explanation: Beans fix nitrogen, improving soil fertility for the next crop.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of crop rotation?
options: B) Breaks pest and disease cycles
quiz.explanation: Rotating crops prevents build-up of pests like weevils and nematodes.

quiz.q: Which of these is a cover crop?
quiz.explanation: Mucuna (velvet bean) is grown to cover soil and add organic matter.

quiz.q: How does mulching help sweet potato farming?
options: B) Conserves moisture and suppresses weeds
quiz.explanation: Mulch keeps soil moist and reduces weed growth.

quiz.q: What is compost made from?
options: B) Kitchen waste, crop residues, and manure
quiz.explanation: Compost is decomposed organic matter, rich in nutrients.

quiz.q: What is required for organic certification?
quiz.explanation: Certifiers require a transition period to ensure no prohibited substances are used.

quiz.q: Which of these is a GAP rule?
options: B) Keep animals in the field
quiz.explanation: Good Agricultural Practices emphasise hygiene to ensure food safety.

quiz.q: What is curing of sweet potatoes?
options: B) Keeping them in warm, humid place for 4-7 days
quiz.explanation: Curing heals cuts and extends shelf life.

quiz.q: Why might a farmer choose organic certification?
quiz.explanation: Organic produce often fetches premium prices in export markets.

quiz.q: What is a buffer zone in organic farming?
options: A) A area to store chemicals
B) A strip of land separating organic and conventional farms
quiz.explanation: Buffer zones prevent chemical drift from neighbouring farms.

quiz.q: What is a cooperative?
options: A) A group of farmers pooling resources
quiz.explanation: Cooperatives help farmers market collectively and access inputs.

quiz.q: How can a cooperative help you get a better price?
options: B) By pooling produce to meet large orders
quiz.explanation: Larger volumes give bargaining power with buyers.

quiz.q: What is contract farming?
options: B) An agreement to sell to a buyer before planting
quiz.explanation: Contract farming reduces market risk by securing a buyer in advance.

quiz.q: Which of these is a value-added sweet potato product?
quiz.explanation: Chips are processed from roots and sell at a higher price.

quiz.q: What is the first step in finding a market?
options: B) Identify potential buyers in your area
quiz.explanation: Knowing who buys and their requirements guides your production.

quiz.q: What should a business plan include?
options: B) Production, marketing, and financial plans
quiz.explanation: A complete plan covers how you will produce, sell, and manage money.

quiz.q: In a business plan, what is a risk plan?
options: A) A list of all possible problems and solutions
quiz.explanation: Risk plan outlines strategies for droughts, pests, or price drops.

quiz.q: Why is a timeline important in a business plan?
options: A) To know when to do each activity
quiz.explanation: A timeline schedules activities from land prep to sales.

quiz.q: What is a realistic yield per acre for sweet potatoes with good practices?
quiz.explanation: With improved varieties and proper management, 8 tonnes per acre is achievable.

quiz.q: What does a break-even analysis tell you?
options: A) The minimum sales needed to cover costs
quiz.explanation: Break-even point is where total revenue equals total costs.
